lines.text: Under this ice, almost four kilometres down, there is a lake. It has been sealed in darkness for millions of years. And in twenty twelve, humans finally touched it.
Some people say it hides a lost ecosystem. Others whisper about secret bases, and creatures from another age. So what is actually down there? And what did the drill really find?
Tonight we keep a drill log. We start on the surface and go down, metre by metre, and every claim gets weighed.
Surface. The ice. The drill. The breakthrough. The life. And finally, the myths. Then a verdict.
Evidence on one side, theory on the other. Let's go down.
Depth zero. The surface. The place is Vostok Station, a Russian base deep in East Antarctica, built in nineteen fifty-seven.
It is one of the coldest places on Earth. The lowest air temperature ever measured at ground level was recorded here, about minus eighty-nine degrees Celsius, in nineteen eighty-three.
In the nineteen sixties, a Russian scientist, Andrei Kapitsa, looked at flight survey data and spotted something odd. Flat, smooth ground under the ice. He suggested there was a lake.
Pilots had already noticed flat, mirror-like radar echoes. The idea sounded absurd. Water, at four kilometres deep, in a land of minus fifty? Most scientists were doubtful.
Then, in nineteen ninety-three, satellite radar altimetry showed a huge, perfectly flat patch on the ice surface above it. That is how a floating ice sheet looks over a lake. The lake was real.
Pressure and the heat of the Earth keep the water liquid. Under that much ice, the melting point drops, and warmth rising from below does the rest.
So we have a real station, a real lake, and a real puzzle. How big is it, and how deep? Next on the log, the ice itself.
Depth, one kilometre and down. The ice. Every layer is a year of snow, pressed into glass. Inside it, tiny bubbles of ancient air.
Scientists drilled one of the deepest ice cores ever made right here, and read the climate of hundreds of thousands of years in it. Ice ages. Warm periods. All recorded in frozen air.
The ice sheet above the lake is about four kilometres thick. The pressure at the bottom is roughly three hundred and fifty times the air pressure at your feet right now.
The lake is long and narrow, about two hundred and fifty kilometres end to end. It is the largest of Antarctica's subglacial lakes, and among the biggest lakes on Earth by volume.
And it is not alone. Radar has now found about four hundred lakes hiding under Antarctic ice. Vostok is simply the giant, and the first we really studied.
The ice slowly slides over the lake, at roughly three metres a year. At the base, lake water freezes onto the ice from below. Scientists call it accretion ice.
That frozen lake water carries tiny traces of what lives or floats below. It is a free sample, delivered from the dark, long before any drill touched the water.
In nineteen ninety-nine, researchers examined that accretion ice and counted microbes. Thousands of cells per millilitre in one study, a few hundred in another. Small numbers, but real ones.
Yet contamination is the great enemy here. A single stray cell from a glove or a drill can ruin everything. That is why this story is full of caution, and full of arguments.
So the ice already gives us hints. But to know the truth, someone had to go through it. Depth next: the drill.
Depth, zero again, but now with a rig. Russian engineers began drilling here in nineteen ninety, through the borehole they called five G.
They used a thermal drill, a hot head that melts ice, and electric cutting heads. Each metre needed pulling the whole string up and down. It took years, with long pauses.
To keep the hole from closing under the pressure, they filled it with a liquid. A kerosene-based fluid, mixed with a freon. Without it, the ice would squeeze the hole shut.
That choice caused real alarm. A hole of oil and chemicals, heading toward a pristine lake. Environmental groups and scientists feared poisoning a world that had never been touched.
Under the Antarctic Treaty, the plan faced scrutiny. Russia argued that the lake water would rise into the hole and push the fluid back, so the lake would stay clean.
They also stopped well above the water, in earlier years. At about three thousand seven hundred metres they paused, to make sure no one cut through blind.
The work was only possible in the short Antarctic summer. In winter, the station is cut off, and temperatures drop so low that planes cannot land. Each season, a few weeks.
Twenty-two years of effort, from the first hole to the last metres. Setbacks. A stuck drill. Funding gaps and political storms. Delay after delay, until the final season.
By early twenty twelve the drill stood just metres above the water. The team knew what could happen. Nobody had done this before.
Depth: almost there. Next on the log: the breakthrough.
The fifth of February, twenty twelve. Late in the Antarctic summer. The crew watched their instruments in the control cabin as the drill went down the final metres.
At three thousand seven hundred and sixty-nine metres, the drill broke through. Reports give about ten twenty-five in the evening, local time. Pressure dropped, and a surge began.
Just as predicted, lake water rushed up the hole. It rose by tens of metres, pushing the drilling fluid ahead of it, and then it froze solid in the cold.
There was relief. Valery Lukin and his team had done it. After more than twenty years, a human hole had reached a lake sealed for perhaps fifteen million years.
But there was no water sample yet. The lake water had frozen in the hole. The team had to wait a full year, then drill again to cut out the frozen plug, in January twenty-thirteen.
That frozen lake water, a few metres of it, is what they brought up. It was mixed with the fluid, so the first job was to figure out what was lake, and what was not.
They returned on the twenty-fifth of January, twenty fifteen, and entered the lake a second time, at about three thousand seven hundred and sixty-nine metres, with a sampling tool.
The head of the expedition promised an honest account. The data would go to peer review. Not every claim would survive that process, and he admitted that.
For the first time in history, humans were in contact with a lake that had been isolated for an unimaginable time. The hole was tiny. The meaning was not.
The water was real. Now the big question. Is anything alive in it? Next on the log.
What lives in a dark lake under four kilometres of ice? The answer, so far, is: very little, and nothing we can prove is new.

In twenty twelve, Russian teams ran DNA tests on the drill-bit water. They found only about ten cells per millilitre. Very few, and four types of bacteria. Three of them came from the drilling fluid itself.
So the first result was disappointing. Mostly contamination. That is science working properly: reporting what looks like life, and then showing it came in with the equipment.

Later work was more interesting. A few years on, a research paper reported DNA of unknown groups, close to families of bacteria such as Burkholderia and Janthinobacterium. Real hints, but not proof of a Vostok ecosystem.
Why not proof? Samples were tiny, mixed with fluid, and handled by many hands. Skeptics said it could all be stray DNA. The lake had not been shown to be a living world, yet.
There is another clue. Studies of the ice suggest the lake could hold a lot of oxygen, released as air bubbles in melting ice slowly dissolve into the water. That is good news for any life.
Extreme conditions. No light. Cold, just below freezing. Huge pressure. Little food. Yet life has been found in places almost like it, from deep ocean vents to other buried lakes.
That is the real excitement. If life can live in a lake like this on Earth, it could live in ice-covered oceans on other worlds, like Jupiter's moon Europa. Vostok is a rehearsal.
That is the honest alien angle. Not creatures in Antarctica, but a test run for how to explore hidden oceans without contaminating them. Space agencies study Vostok for exactly that reason.
So life? Maybe tiny. Maybe nothing. The evidence is thin. And then there are the myths. Next on the log.
Now the stories. Hidden Nazi base. Alien bunker. A lost world of dinosaurs. They all say the same thing: something is being hidden at Vostok.

The Nazi base story grows from a real German expedition to Antarctica in nineteen thirty-eight and thirty-nine. It claimed a patch of land. It did not build a secret city under four kilometres of ice.
The monster version says a creature lives in the lake, left from an earlier age. No evidence. A lake of near-freezing water, under that pressure, offers no food for large animals.
The cover-up version says officials stopped science from looking. In reality, the opposite happened. Teams from several countries studied it, published papers, and argued in public for decades.
And the alien story? It draws on the lake's strangeness and a few bad satellite pictures of ice formations. There is no craft, no signal, no object. Only a very remote scientific site.
The truth is stranger in a quieter way. A hidden lake, real water, real pressure, almost no life. Time to score the lake.
The drill is back on the surface. The log is closed. Let us look at what we have.
Debrief. Time to score Lake Vostok.
A huge liquid lake under four kilometres of ice: evidence. Reached by drilling in twenty twelve, and again in twenty fifteen: evidence. Oxygen-rich, dark, cold: likely.
A thriving hidden ecosystem: unproven. A Nazi or alien base: no evidence. A monster in the lake: debunked. A cover-up: contradicted by the open record.

The verdict. The lake is real and the discovery is real. The aliens, bases and monsters are not. But the real question, whether anything lives there, is still open, and that is more thrilling than any myth.
Somewhere under that ice, dark water is moving, slowly, in a place no light has ever reached. We keep hunting for strange worlds out in space. This one is right here on Earth.
Next case: a lump of polished crystal, three thousand years old, found in an Assyrian palace. Was it a telescope?
Do you think anything lives in Lake Vostok? Tell us in the comments, and subscribe for the next ancient mystery put to the test.
